content.title: About
content.content: Bean sprouts are the young shoots of soybeans that retain a crisp texture and mild flavor after cooking. Cooked sprouts are commonly used in Asian cuisines, soups, and salads. They are rich in vitamins, minerals, and plant protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bean sprouts are a staple in Japanese, Chinese, and Thai dishes.
When boiled for 5‑7 minutes they keep most of their nutrients without becoming mushy.
In Japan cooked sprouts are often served as a side dish with rice.
Vitamin C content in bean sprouts is higher than in many other vegetables.
You can grow sprouts at home from dry beans in 3‑5 days.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and enhances iron absorption.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Protein from bean sprouts aids tissue repair and helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked sprouts contains fewer than 30 calories, making them ideal for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: High in folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important for pregnant women.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw sprouts can harbor salmonella; cooking them to a boil reduces this risk.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may react to bean sprouts.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large portions may cause gas and bloating.

items.title: Oxalic acid content
items.content: Oxalic acid can interfere with calcium absorption if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked bean sprouts can be added to soups, stir‑fries, salads, and spring rolls. They are often quickly sautéed with garlic and soy sauce, or served as a side dish with rice or noodles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked sprouts in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if they develop an off‑odor or slimy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Ground beef is finely chopped meat obtained from various cuts of a cow. A patty made from this ground beef is a shaped portion, usually pan‑fried or baked. The product has a rich meaty flavor, firm texture, and high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ground beef is a staple in many national dishes, from American burgers to Italian Bolognese sauce.
Beef patties can be seasoned with herbs, spices, and vegetables for varied taste profiles.
Traditionally the grind comes from shoulder, neck, or round cuts, which provide a balance of lean meat and fat for juiciness.
In some cultures beef is considered a “leaner” option compared with pork because of its lower saturated‑fat content.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Ground beef supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals aid immune function and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Beef naturally contains creatine, beneficial for muscle strength and endurance.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Ground beef can be high in saturated fat; choosing lean varieties helps limit intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw meat may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella or E. coli; cook to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Pre‑packaged ground beef may contain preservatives, flavor enhancers, or fillers that not everyone tolerates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef patties can be pan‑fried over medium heat until a golden crust forms, baked in the oven, or grilled. Serve with vegetables, sauces, in burgers, or use in stews and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ground beef refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container at ‑18 °C, where it remains good for 3‑4 months. Thaw frozen meat in the refrigerator before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef, roast, hash is a dish made from finely chopped boiled or roasted beef, sautéed with onion, carrot, and spices. It is often served with mashed potatoes or bread and has a rich, savory flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “hash” comes from the French “hacher” meaning “to chop finely.”
The dish is popular in the United States and Canada, frequently served as a breakfast item.
Traditional recipes used beef tail, but today more common cuts are used for convenience.
Hash is often cooked in large pots, which helps retain the meat’s juiciness.
It is believed to have originated in the 19th century as a way to use leftover meat.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Heme iron from beef is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Natural creatine in beef helps supply energy to muscles.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Excessive intake may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Adding salt or soy sauce can make the dish overly salty.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Improper cooking can lead to salmonella or E. coli contamination.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience an allergic reaction.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hash hot, often with a side of mashed potatoes, rice, or fresh vegetables. Adding poached eggs or cheese can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked hash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Macaroni with cheese is a dish of boiled pasta coated in a creamy cheese sauce. It is often made with short pasta shapes (elbow, shells) and uses grated cheddar, parmesan, or a blend of cheeses. The dish is popular in children's meals and as a quick dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century as “macaroni and cheese” and quickly became a comfort‑food classic.
There are more than 30 sauce variations, ranging from classic cheddar to blue‑cheese or cream‑mustard blends.
In Russia, macaroni with cheese is frequently baked in the oven until a golden crust forms.
The cheese sauce can be made with milk, cream, or even plant‑based milk for a vegetarian version.
It is a staple in school cafeterias because it is fast to prepare and nutritionally dense.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pasta provides complex carbohydrates that release energy slowly, supporting sustained activity.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cheese adds high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cheese sauce supplies calcium for bone health and small amounts of vitamin D.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both pasta and cheese contribute B12, riboflavin, and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber (when using whole‑grain pasta)
items.content: Whole‑grain macaroni adds fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese sauces can be rich in saturated fats, which may increase cardiovascular risk if eaten frequently.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheeses often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The dish may cause discomfort for those who cannot digest lactose; lactose‑free alternatives can be used.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to dairy proteins.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Macaroni with cheese is relatively calorie‑dense, so portions should be controlled, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, topped with extra grated cheese and fresh herbs. You can add ham, bacon, vegetables (broccoli, peas) or spices (paprika, black pepper) for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk or cream to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetables are a diverse group of edible plant parts – roots, leaves, stems and fruits – that are commonly used in curry to add flavor, texture and nutritional value. Traditional Indian and Asian curry recipes often feature potatoes, carrots, cauliflower, eggplant, spinach, tomatoes and peas.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetables in curry create a balance of sweetness, bitterness and heat.
The oldest curry recipes from the 12th century already included peas and pumpkin.
Different regions use characteristic local vegetables: southern India favors coconut and sweet potato, North Africa uses carrot and turnip.
Simmering vegetables in the sauce retains more vitamins than boiling them in water.
Vegetables make curry more affordable and suitable for vegetarian diets.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamins A, C, K and B‑complex, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, helps regulate blood sugar and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Most vegetables have low energy density, making vegetable‑rich curry suitable for weight management.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Pigments such as beta‑carotene and lycopene protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Potassium, magnesium and iron in vegetables support heart and muscle function.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific vegetables, such as tomatoes or eggplant.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Improperly washed vegetables can retain pesticide residues.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Vegetables like spinach and beetroot are high in oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stones in susceptible people.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Certain vegetables (e.g., legumes) can cause gas if not soaked and cooked properly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add vegetables to curry at different stages: root vegetables early for softness, leafy greens near the end to preserve color and aroma. Cut them into cubes, slices or grate them. For a milder flavor, pre‑roast or sauté the vegetables before mixing into the sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Cooked vegetable curry should be kept in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. Frozen vegetables retain quality for up to 6 months; thaw quickly before adding to the sauce.
